title: The Cost-Per-Cup Gap: Why Rising Coffee Prices Haven't Made It Onto the Menu Board Yet
linkedin:
A kilo of coffee beans costs more today than it did a year ago. The price on most café menu boards hasn't moved to match it.

That gap is where café margin quietly disappears, cup by cup, long before anyone thinks to go looking for it.

Here's the part that catches most owners out. A flat white's true cost is never just the bean. Milk, the cup and lid, wastage from a failed pour and the power running the machine all move in roughly the same direction as wholesale bean prices, usually within the same twelve months. The menu price only moves when an owner makes a deliberate call to move it, and for most cafés that happens once a year at best.

So beverage cost percentage creeps upward in small, almost invisible steps while revenue keeps looking perfectly healthy on the P&L. Revenue can hold steady while the margin underneath it quietly narrows, and a monthly report rarely flags that kind of movement until someone checks for it specifically.

The hesitation to reprice is rarely about the maths. It's the worry about what a loyal regular says when their usual order costs more than last visit, and the sense that a small rise looks petty against years of goodwill.

That instinct is reasonable. But it leaves the gap between cost and price open far longer than the cost increase itself took to arrive, and a few cents a cup adds up fast once you multiply it across a trading week.

Noticed your coffee bean invoice creeping up this year but haven't touched the price on the board?

You're not alone, and it's not carelessness. Most café owners can do the maths on a ten cent increase in seconds. What actually holds the price in place is the worry about what a loyal regular says when their usual order costs more than it did last time.

Here's the catch. While the price sits still, milk, wastage and power costs are usually moving in the same direction as the bean price, all year. So the margin on every cup quietly narrows while revenue looks exactly the same as always.

Worth a look at your actual cost per cup before the next trading week. What's stopped you from adjusting yours?

A note for café and hospitality owners across Brisbane, the Gold Coast, Sunshine Coast and the wider east coast this Australian Small Business Month.

With International Coffee Day just behind us, it's worth a closer look at something many café owners haven't checked in a while: whether menu prices have kept pace with what coffee actually costs to make. Wholesale bean prices have moved over the past couple of years, and milk, wastage and running costs tend to move in the same direction. Menu prices, by contrast, often stay fixed for a year or more simply because repricing feels like a bigger decision than it is.

The result is a beverage cost percentage that creeps upward quietly while revenue looks steady, hiding a margin that is narrowing underneath it. A gap of a few cents a cup sounds small until it is multiplied across a full trading week and every coffee based drink on the menu.

If you haven't checked your own cost per cup against your current prices recently, it's a useful twenty minutes before the next quiet trading period. Read the full piece on the ProfitPulse blog for a clearer way to work through it.
